extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, taxonomists, historians of science, and readers interested in scientific practice
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and expectations for doing detailed taxonomic/monographic work, conducting observational anatomy/development studies, and for scientific naming/nomenclature practices in natural history. Includes guidance on methods, evidence, and professional conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of detailed monographic work as systematic training
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cirripede monograph was 'a piece of critical self-discipline' and its value lay not merely in the addition to positive knowledge but in the systematic training and discipline it gave, which manifested itself in all later writings and saved the author from endless errors of detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long, painstaking monographic work (careful dissection, detailed plates, extensive indices) is to be valued as essential training for reliable speculative and synthetic work; it strengthens method and critical judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire anatomy and developmental knowledge for taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: After his return it was necessary for him to gain 'a corresponding acquaintance with Anatomy and Development, and their relation to Taxonomy' which he 'acquired by his Cirripede work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplement observational and theoretical study with practical training in anatomy and embryology/physiology to underpin taxonomic and evolutionary arguments; such training would have strengthened later chapters in synthetic works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of accepted facts and avoid purely deductive use
rubrics_metrics.description: The great danger is 'the temptation to deal with the accepted statements of facts in natural science, as if they were not only correct, but exhaustive; as if they might be dealt with deductively, in the same way as propositions in Euclid may be dealt with.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat accepted facts as contingent on means of observation and viewpoint; avoid over-extending speculative deductions beyond what empirical support can bear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect honest, thorough descriptive/cataloguing work
rubrics_metrics.description: Would never allow a depreciatory remark to pass unchallenged on the poorest class of scientific workers, provided that their work was honest, and good of its kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value 'digging out synonyms' and thorough description even when unglamorous; such labor improves methods and understanding of difficulties in cataloguing and systematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species descriptions should discuss affinities, structure, range and habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of many short descriptions: papers with short descriptions of species 'without one word on their affinities, internal structure, range or habits' are inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good taxonomic papers should go beyond mere naming/descriptions to address relationships (affinities), internal anatomy/structure, geographic range, and natural history/habits to be scientifically useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'naming instead of describing' — oppose vanity-driven authorship on species names
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of appending for perpetuity the name of the first describer to species is seen as 'a direct premium to hasty work, to NAMING instead of DESCRIBING.' A species ought to have a name so well known that the addition of the author's name would be superfluous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage practices that reward hurried naming; prefer thorough descriptions and stable names, and consider citing systematic authorities rather than perpetually appending first-describer names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply nomenclatural rules pragmatically — priority can harm stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the rules (e.g., of priority) are 'very useful' to rest upon, strict adherence (reviving obscure earlier names) 'would do more harm than good,' since newly fished-up names would not be adopted and could cause confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established nomenclatural rules for stability, but exercise practical judgement when strict priority would introduce confusing or unused names; consider likelihood of adoption and overall clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate methods and instruments for anatomical observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the work was done with a simple dissecting microscope, but the need for higher powers induced purchase of a compound microscope; detailed dissection and many plates/figures were produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ the necessary techniques and magnification for the scale of the structures under study (e.g., dissections, appropriate microscopes), and produce sufficient illustrative plates/figures and indices to document work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative observation produces insight and pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'an extraordinary pleasure in pure observation' often derived from 'comparisons forming in one's mind with allied structures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate close comparative observation of allied forms as a route to discovering structure, function, and relationships; intellectual enjoyment reinforces careful empirical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider relative reliability of different kinds of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference (in some cases) for 'pure geological evidence' over zoological or botanical evidence when the former is simpler; one should not prefer poor geological evidence to good organic evidence but geological reasoning can be more straightforward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess evidence types critically and weigh their relative simplicity and directness; geological data may provide clearer inferences in some contexts, but quality of evidence should dominate choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use codes/rules of nomenclature as stabilizing frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: The nomenclature rules published (e.g., in the British Association Transactions) are 'very useful' and 'a comfort to have something to rest on in the turbulent ocean of nomenclature,' though difficult to obey always.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt and consult established codes of nomenclature to provide consistency and a basis for resolving disputes, while acknowledging practical difficulties and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional conduct: favour collaboration over specimen-hoarding
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdote criticizing collectors who aimed only at 'filling their cabinets with rare things' and the 'pettiness of collectors' who kept specimens selfishly rather than contributing to collective works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote cooperative behavior: share specimens and data for collective knowledge (e.g., local faunas, museums) rather than hoarding material for personal vanity or priority.
